sentences.text: The 33 sermons on Nibbana were delivered by the Venerable Bhikkhu Katukurunde Jnanananda in Sinhala at Mitrigala Nisarana Vinaya Forest Hermitage.
They were translated into English by the same Venerable monk, presently residing at Potkulkala Forest Hermitage in Khandagedra, Devalagam.
This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.
With the permission of the Most Venerable Great Preceptor and the assembly of the Venerable Meditative Monks, this is the 20th sermon in the series of sermons on Nibbana.

In our last sermon, we described as something of a marvel in the attainment of Nibbana, the very possibility of realizing in this very life as Ditra Dhammika, once after death state, which is Samparai.

The phrase Ditra Dhammika, having realized here and now by one's own higher knowledge, occurs so often in the discourses because the emancipated one ascertains his after death state as if by seeing with his own eyes.
Nathidani punabhavo, there is no re-becoming now.
Khenajati, extinctice birth, are some of the joyous utterances of the Buddha and the Arans, which were inspired by the realization of the cessation of existence in this very life.
Through that realization itself, they experience a bliss divide of feeling, which is called the cooling off of feelings.
That is why Nibbana, as such, is known as Avedaita Sukha, a bliss divide of feeling.
At the end of their lives, when the moment of death approaches, those emancipated ones, the Arans, put forward their unshakable deliverance of the mind,
akuppa, which remains unshakable, even in the face of death, and become deathless well before their death, not after it.
On many an occasion, the Buddha has spoken highly of this unshakable deliverance of the mind, describing it as the supreme bliss, the supreme knowledge, and the supreme freedom from death.
For instance, among the sixes of the Anguttara Nikaya, we come across the following two verses.
To that such like one, who is fully released, there arises the knowledge, unshakable is my deliverance, upon his extinction of fetters to existence.
This is the highest knowledge, this is the unsurpassed bliss, this sorrowless, taintless security, is the supreme debtlessness.
Arans are said to be debtless in regard to the four requisites offered by the laity out of faith, but when Nibbana is regarded as a debtlessness, it seems to imply something deeper.
Saṃsāra or reiterated existence is itself a debt which one can never pay off.
When one comes to think of kamma and its result, it is a debt that keeps on gathering an interminable interest which can never be paid off.
But even from this debt, the Arans have won freedom by destroying the seeds of kamma, by rendering them infertile.
They are made ineffective beyond this life as there is no rebirth.
The meaningful line of the Ratanasutt, Khinang, Puranang, Navang, Nathisambhavam, whatever is old, is extinct and there is no arising anew, has to be understood in that sense.
The coming debt is paid off and there is no fresh incurring.
So, all this is in praise of that unshakable deliverance of the mind.
It is a kind of extraordinary knowledge, almost unimaginable, a realization of one's own after-death state.
In almost all serious discussions on Nibbana, the subtlest mood point turns out to be the question of the after-death state, the emancipated one.
A brief answer the Buddha had given to this question, we are already brought up in our last sermon by quoting the two concluding verses of the Udhāna,
with which that collection of inspired utterances ends with a note of exceptional grandeur.
Let us recall them.
Just as in the case of a fire blazing like a block of iron in point of compactness, when it gradually calms down, no path it goes by can be traced.
Even so, of those who are well released, who have crossed over the floods of shackles of sensuality and reached bliss unshaken, there is no path to be pointed out.
The last two lines are particularly significant.
There is no path to be pointed out of those who have reached bliss unshaken.
Achalang Sukhan, or unshakable bliss, is none other than that unshakable deliverance of the mind.
Akupa means unassailable or unshakable.
Clearly enough, what the verse says is that after their death, the emancipated ones leave no trace of a path gone by, even as the flames of a raging fire.
The flame may appear as something really existing due to the perception of the compact, ghana-sanya, but when it goes down and disappears, no one can say that it went in such and such a direction.
Though this is the obvious meaning, some try to attribute quite a different meaning to the verse in question.

The line, there is no path to be pointed out, is interpreted even by the commentators, who take the word gati to mean some state of existence as an assertion that although such a wound cannot be pointed out, the arahans pass away into some nondescript realm.
This kind of interpretation is prompted by an apprehension of the charge of annihilation.
A clear instance of this tendency is revealed in the commentary to the following verse in the Dhammapada.
Innocent are the sages that are ever restrained in body.
They go to that state unshaken wherein they grieve no more.
The commentator, in paraphrasing, brings in the word satsatam, eternal, for achutam, thereby giving the idea that the arahans go to an eternal place of rest.
Because the verb yanti, go, occurs there, he must have thought that this state unshaken, achutam, is something attainable after death.
But we can give another instance in support of our explanation of the term achutam.
The following verse in the Hemakamānava-puccha of Parāyana-vagga in the Sutta Nipātha clearly shows what this achutam is.
That dispelling here in this world of desire and lust in pleasurable things, seen, heard, sensed and cognized, is Nibbāna itself, O Hemakam.
This is further proof of the fact that there is no eternal, immortal rest awaiting the arahans after their demise.
The reason for such a postulate is probably the fear of falling into an annihilationist view.
Why this chronic fear?
To the worldlings overcome by the cravings for existence?
Any teaching that leads to the cessation of existence appears dreadful.
That is why they put forward two new parables following the same commentarial trend.
The other day we mentioned about those two parables, the parable of the tortoise and the parable of the frog.
When the fish and the toad living in water ask what sort of...
thing land is, the tortoise and the frog are forced to say no-no to every question they put.
Likewise, the Buddha, so it is argued, was forced to give a string of negative terms
in his discourses on Nibbana. But we have pointed out that this argument is fallacious
and that those discourses have to be interpreted differently. The theme that runs through such
discourses is none other than the cessation of existence. In the Aragadvyupama Sutta of the
Majjmanikaya, the Buddha declares, in unmistakable terms, that some recluses and brahmins on hearing
him preaching the Dhamma for the cessation of existence, wrongly accuse him with the charge
of being an annihilationist. Sato sattas uccedaṁ vināsaṁ vibhāṁ panyapit, he is showing the
way to the annihilation, destruction and nonexistence of a truly existing being. He clearly states
that some even grieve and lament and fall into despair, complaining,
urchajyaṁ sāmi nāmasu, vināsaṁ sāmi nāmasu, nasu nāma bhavi sāmi, so it seems I shall be
annihilated, so it seems I shall perish, so it seems I shall be no more.
Even during the lifetime of the Buddha, there were various debates and controversies regarding
the after-death state of the emancipated person among recluses and brahmins. They were of the
opinion that the after-death state of the emancipated one in any particular religious system has to be
explained according to a fourfold logic or tetralemma. A paradigm of that tetralemma occurs quite often in
the discourses. It consists of the following four propositions.

The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma exists after death. The tetralemma
to round up the four possible alternatives in any situation or four possible answers
to any question. The dilemma is fairly well known where one is caught up between two alternatives.
The tetralemma with its four alternatives is supposed to exhaust the universe of discourse
in a way that one cannot afford to ignore it. When it comes to a standpoint regarding
a particular issue, one is compelled to say yes or no, or at least to assert both standpoints
or negate them altogether. The contemporary recluses and brahmins held on to the bibb
that the Tathagata's after death state has to be predicated in accordance with the four
cornered logic. When we hear the term Tathagata, we are immediately reminded of the Buddha,
but for the contemporary society, it was a sort of technical term with a broader meaning.
Those recluses and brahmins used the term Tathagata to designate the perfected individual in any
religious system, whose qualifications were summed up in the thematic phrase Uttama Puriso,
Parampuriso, Paramapattipattu, the highest person, the supreme person, the one who has attained
the supreme state. This fact is clearly borne out by the Kuthuhala Sala Sutta in the Avhyagata
Sanyutta, the Sanyutta Nikaya. In that discourse, we find the wandering ascetic Vachagata coming
to the Buddha with the following report. Recently, there was a meeting of recluses, brahmins and
wandering ascetics in the debating hall. In that assembly, the following chants talk eros.
Now, there is his teacher, Purana Kasappa, who is widely acclaimed and who has a large following.
When an ordinate disciple of his passes away, he predicates his destiny. So also, in the
case of a disciple who has attained the highest state of perfection in his religious system.
Other well-known teachers like Makkhali Gosala, Niganthanathaputta, Sanjayabelattiputta, Pakudhakacchayana
and Ajitakesakambali do the same. They all declare categorically the after-death state of both
types of their disciples. But as for this ascetic Gautama, who also is a teacher widely acclaimed,
with a large following, the position is that he clearly declares the after-death state of an ordinary
disciple of his. But in the case of a disciple who has attained the highest state of perfection,
he does not predicate his destiny according to the above-mentioned tetralema. Instead,
he makes such a declaration about him as the following, Accajitthanham vabattai sanyojanam sammamana
abhisamya antamakasi dukkhasya. He cut off grieving, disjoyed the fetter, and by rightly understanding
concede for what it is, made an end of suffering. Accagatya concludes this account with the confession
that he himself was perplexed and was in doubt as to how the dhamma of the recluse Gautama has to be
understood. The Buddha grants that Vajcagatya's doubt is reasonable with the words,
alanghite vajca kankhitum, alangmichikichitum, kankhanie panate thani kankha upanna.
It behoves you to doubt, vajca, it behoves you to be perplexed, for doubt has arisen in you on a
dubious point. Then the Buddha comes out with the correct standpoint in order to dispel Vajcagatya's
doubt, saupadhanas khaaham vajca upatting panya pemi no anupadhanas. It is for one with grasping,
Vajcagatya declare there is an occurrence of birth, not for one without grasping. He gives the following
simile by way of illustration. Sa yathapi vajca aggi saupadhano jalati no anupadhano.
Eva me eva khaaham vajca saupadhanas upatting panya pemi no anupadhanas. Just as a fire burns
when it has failed to grasp and not when it has no fear, even so, vajca, I declare that there is an
occurrence of birth for one with grasping, not for one without grasping. As we have mentioned before,
the word upadhan has two meanings. It means both grasping as well as fear. In fact,
fear is just what the fire grasps. Just as the fire depends on grasping in the form of fuel,
so also the individual depends on grasping for his rebirth. Within the context of this analogy,
Vajcagatya now raises a question that has some deeper implications.
Master Gautama, at the time when a flame flung by the wind goes even far, what does Master Gautama
declare to be its object of grasping or fear? The Buddha's answer to that question is,
Asmingko vajca sameyi achi vateen khitta durampi gacchati, tamhaam vatupadhanam vadhani,
vatohissa vajca tasming sameyi upadhanam hoti. At the time vajca, a flame flung by the wind goes even far,
that I say has wind as its object of grasping. Vajcagatya at that time, wind itself serves as the object of grasping.
Now, this is only an analogy, which raises the question proper only at this point.
Yasmin cha Panabho Gautama samye ima cha kāyāng nikhipati satto cha anyatarang kāyāng anuppatto goti ima cha Panabhavam Gautama king upadāna saming panyapeti.
At the time, Master Gautama, a being lays down this body and has freed a certain body.
What does Master Gautama declare to be a grasping in his case?
The Buddha replies, At the time, a being lays down this body and has freed a certain body, I say he has craving as is grasping.
At that time, it is craving that serves as grasping for him.
With this sentence, the discourse ends abruptly, but there is an intricate point in the two sections quartered above.
In these two sections, we have adopted the reading anuppatto as more plausible in rendering the phrase anyatarang kāyāng anuppatto has read a certain body.
The commentary, however, seeks to justify the reading anuppatto is not reborn, which gives quite an opposite sense.
With the following explanation,
Chutikkhane yeva patisandhi kittas anuppannata anuppanno hoti.
Since at the death moment itself, the rebirth consciousness has not yet risen, he is said to be not yet reborn.
Some editors doubt whether the correct reading should be anuppatto.
The doubt seems reasonable enough.
For even syntactically, anuppatto can be shown to fit into the context better than anuppanno.
The word anyatarang provides us with the criterion.
It has a selective sense, like a certain.
udi-sanKayakona
Thank you.
and carries definite positive implications. To express something negative, a word like anyang, another, has to be used instead of the selective anyatarang, a certain.

On the other hand, the suggested reading, Anupattu, avoids those syntactical difficulties. A being lays down this body and has raised a certain body. Even the simile given as an illustration is in favor of our interpretation.

The original question of watcher about the flame flung by the wind reminds us of the way a forest fire, for instance, spreads from one tree to another tree some distance away. It is the wind that pushes the flame for it to catch hold of the other tree.

The commentarial explanation, however, envisages a situation in which a being lays down this body and is not yet reborn in another body. It is in the interim that craving is supposed to be a grasping or a fear.
Some scholars have exploited this commentarial explanation to postulate a theory of antarabhava or interim existence prior to rebirth proper.
Our interpretation, based on the reading, Anupattu, ruled out even the possibility of an antarabhava.
Obviously enough, watcher's question is simple and straightforward.
He is curious to know what sort of a grasping connects up the being that lays down the body and the being that arises in another body.
That is to say, how the apparent gap could be built.
The answer given by the Buddha fully accords with the analogy envisaged by the premise.
Just as the wind does the work of grasping in the case of the flame, so craving itself at the moment of death fulfills the function of grasping for a being to reach another body.
That is precisely why craving is called bhavanetti, the guide in becoming.
Like a promontory, it juts out into the ocean of samsara.
When it comes to rebirth, it is craving that bridges the apparent gap.
It is the invisible combustible fuel that keeps the raging samsaric forest fire alive.
All in all, what transpired at the debating hall reveals one important fact,
namely, that the Buddha's reluctance to give a categorical answer regarding the after-death state of the emancipated one in his dispensation
had aroused the curiosity of those recluses and brahmins.
That is why they kept on discussing the subject at length.
However, it was not the fact that he had refused to make any comment at all on this point.
Only that the comment he had made appeared so strange to them,
as we may well infer from Vacha's report of the discussion at the debating hall.
The Buddha's comment on the subject, which they had courted, was not based on the tetralema.
It was a completely new formulation.
Acha chitanhaṁ vāvattai sanyojanāṁ sammā māna abhisamyaṁ antamakāsi dukkhasu.
The cut-off craving disjoined the fetter,
and by rightly understanding conceit for what it is, made an end of suffering.
This, then, is the correct answer, and not any one of the four corners of the tetralema.
This brief formula is of paramount importance.
When craving is cut off, the guide in becoming, which is responsible for rebirth, is done away with.
It is as if the fetter binding to another existence has been unhooked.
The term bhavasanyojanākha, destruction of the fetter to existence, we came across earlier, conveys the same sense.
The phrase, ammā māna abhisamyaṁ is also highly significant.
With the dispelling of ignorance, the conceit, am, asmi māna, is seen for what it is.
It disappears when exposed to the light of understanding, and that is the end of suffering as well.
The concluding phrase, antamakāsi dukkhasu, made an end of suffering, is conclusive enough.
The problem that was there all the time was the problem of suffering.
So the end of suffering means the end of the whole problem.
In the aggiva-chagapta-sutta of the majjhmanikāya, the Buddha's response to the question of the after-death state of the arahantra comes to light in greater detail.
The question is presented there in the form of the tetra-lemmā, beginning with hoti-tathāgato-param-marāna.
While all the other recluses and brahmins held that the answer should necessarily take the form of one of the four alternatives,
the Buddha put them all aside, thapitāni, rejected them, patikhitāni, refused to state his view categorically in terms of them, avyākatāni.
This attitude of the Buddha puzzled not only the ascetics of other sects, but even some of the monks like Malumkeputta.
In very strong terms, Malumkeputta challenged the Buddha to give a categorical answer or else confess his ignorance.
As a matter of fact, there are altogether ten questions which the Buddha laid aside, rejected and refused to answer categorically.
The first six take the form of three dilemmas, while the last four constitute the tetra-lemmā already mentioned.
Since an examination of those three dilemmas would reveal some important facts, we shall briefly discuss their significance as well.
The three sets of views are stated thematically as follows.
Sassato loko, the world is eternal, asassato loko, the world is not eternal, antava loko, the world is finite, anantava loko, the world is infinite,
tang jīvang tang sarirang, the soul and the body are the same, anyang jīvang anyang sarirang, the soul is one thing and the body another.
These three dilemmas together with the tetra-lemmā are known as avyākatāvatthūni, the ten undetermined points.
Various recluses and brahmins, as well as king Pasenati Kosala, posed these ten questions to the Buddha, hoping to get categorical answers.
Why the Buddha laid them aside is a problem to many scholars.
Some, like Malukya Buddha, would put it down to agnosticism.
Others would claim that the Buddha laid them aside because they are relevant to the immediate problem of deliverance, though he could have answered them.
That section of opinion go by the Singsapa Sutta in the Satcha Sanyutta or Sanyuttanikāt.
Once, while dwelling in a Singsapa grove, the Buddha took up some Singsapa leaves in his hand and asked the monks,
What do you think, monks, which is more, these leaves in my hand or those in the Singsapa grove?
The monks replied that the leaves in the hand are few and those in the Singsapa grove are greater in number.
Then the Buddha makes the declaration to the following effect.
Even so, monks, what I have understood through higher knowledge and not taught you is far more than what I have taught you.
If we rely on this simile, we would have to grant that the questions are answerable in principle,
but that the Buddha prefer to avoid them because they are not relevant.
But this is not the reason either.
All these ten questions are based on wrong premises.
To take them seriously and answer them would be to grant the validity of those premises.
The dilemmas and the tetralemma seek arbitrarily to corner anyone who tries to answer them.
The Buddha refuse to be cornered that way.
The first two alternatives presented in the form of a dilemma are
Sassato Loko, the world is eternal, and Asassato Loko, the world is not eternal.
This is an attempt to determine the world in temporal terms.
The next set of alternatives seeks to determine the world in spatial terms.
Why did the Buddha refuse to answer these questions on time and space?
It is because the concept of the world has been given quite a new definition in this dispensation.
Whenever the Buddha redefined a word in common usage, he introduced it with the phrase
Aryasa Vinay, in the discipline of the noble ones.
We have already mentioned on an earlier occasion that according to the discipline of the noble ones,
the world is said to have arisen in the six sense spheres, chasu loko samukpanna.
In short, the world is redefined in terms of the six spheres of sense.
This is so fundamentally important that in the Salayatana Samyatta of the Samyatta Nikaya,
the theme comes up again and again.
For instance, in the Samiddhi Sutta, Venerable Samiddhi poses the following question to the Buddha.
Loko, loko ti bhante buccati, titta avatanu gho bhante, loko va asa, loka panyakti vaa.
The world, the world, so it is said, Venerable Sir.
But how far, Venerable Sir, does this world or the concept of the world go?
So, the Buddha gives the following answer.
Yathakho Samiddhi, Atthi Chakhu, Atthi Rupa, Atthi Chakhu Vinyana, Atthi Chakhu Vinyatabba Dhamma, Atthi Tathya Loko Va, Loka Panyakti Va.
Where there is the I Samiddhi, where there are forms, where there is I Consciousness,
where there are things colonizable by I Consciousness, there exists the world or the concept of the world.
A similar statement is made with regard to the other spheres of science.
including the mind. That, according to the Buddha, is where the world exists. Then he
makes a declaration concerning the converse. Yathakho samiddhi nathe chakku, nathe rupa,
nathe chakku iññāna, nathe chakku iññāta badhamma, nathe tattha lokuva loka paññativa.
Where there is no I samiddhi, where there are no forms, where there is no I consciousness,
where there are no things cognizable by I consciousness, there the world does not exist nor any concept
of the world. From this we can well infer that any attempt to determine whether there is an
end of the world, either in temporal terms or in spatial terms, is misguided. It is the
outcome of a wrong grip, for there is a world so long as there are the six spheres of sense.
That is why the Buddha consistently refused to answer those questions regarding the world.
There are a number of definitions of the world given by the Buddha. We shall cite two of them.
A certain monk directly asked the Buddha to give a definition of the world.
The world, the world, the world, so it is said, in what respect, Venerable Sir, is it called
the world? Then the Buddha makes the following significant declaration.
It is disintegrating monk. That is why it is called the world. And what does the world mean?
What is disintegrating? The I monk is disintegrating. Forms are disintegrating. Eye consciousness is
disintegrating. Eye contact is disintegrating. And whatever feeling that arises dependent on
eye contact, be it pleasant or painful, or neither pleasant nor painful, that too is disintegrating.
It is disintegrating. That is why it is called the world. Here the Buddha is redefining the concept
of the world, punning on the verb Lujjati, which means to break up or disintegrate, to bring
about a radical change in outlook in accordance with the Dhamma. The Buddha would sometimes introduce
a new etymology in preference to the old. This definition of the world is to the same effect.
Venerable Ananda too raises the same question, soliciting a redefinition for the well-known
concept of the world. And the Buddha responds with the following answer.
Whatever Ananda is subject to disintegration, that is called the world in the noble one's discipline.
He even goes on to substantiate his statement at length.
And what Ananda is subject to disintegration? The I, Ananda, is subject to disintegration.
Forms are subject to disintegration. Eye consciousness is subject to disintegration.
Eye contact is subject to disintegration.
And whatever feeling that arises dependent on eye contact, be it pleasant or painful,
or neither present nor painful, that too is subject to disintegration.
Whatever is subject to disintegration, Ananda is called the world in the noble one's discipline.
In this instance, the play upon the word loka is vividly apt in that it brings out the transiency
of the world. If the world, by definition, is regarded as transient, it cannot be conceived
substantially as a unit. How then can any eternity or infinity be predicated about it?
If all the so-called things in the world listed above are all the time disintegrating, any unitary
concept of the world is fallacious. Had the Buddha answered those misconceived questions, he
would thereby concede to the wrong concept of the world current among the other religious groups.
So then we can understand why the Buddha refused to answer the first four questions.
Now let us examine the next dilemma. Thang Jeevang Thang Sarirang Anyang Jeevang Anyang Sarirang
The soul and the body are the same. The soul is one thing and the body another.
To these questions also the other religionists insisted on a categorical answer, either yes
or no. There is a catch in the way these questions are framed. The Buddha refused to get called
to them. These two questions are of the type that clever lawyers put to a respondent these
days. They would sometimes insist strictly on a yes or no as answer and ask a question
like, have you now given up drinking? If the respondent happens to be a tea-toteller, he
would be in a quandary, since both answers tend to create a wrong impression. So also in
the case of these two alternatives, the soul and the body are the same, the soul is one
thing and the body another. Either way there is a presumption of a soul which the Buddha did
not subscribe to. The Buddha had unequivocally declared that the idea of a soul is the outcome
of an utterly foolish view. Kevalo Paripuro Baladhammo. That is why the Buddha rejected both
standpoints. A similar catch, a similar misconception underlies the tetralemma concerning the after-death
state of the Tathagata. It should be already clear to some extent by what we have discussed
so far. For the Buddha, the term Tathagata had a different connotation than what it meant
for those of other sex. The latter adhered to the view that both the ordinary disciple as
well as the perfected individual in their systems of thought had a soul of some description or
other. The Buddha never subscribed to such a view. On the other hand, he invested the term
Tathagata with an extremely deep and subtle meaning. Its definition of the term will emerge
from the Agivacchavata-sutta which we propose to discuss now. In this discourse, we find the
wandering ascetic watcher trying to get a categorical answer to the questioner, putting each of the
the questions with legal precision, one by one, as a lawyer would at the courts of law.
Kinnagho bho Gotama sasato loko idame vasachyam mo bhamanyanti evang dithi bhavang Gotama.
Now, Master Gotama, the world is eternal. This only is true. All else is false. Are you of this view,
Master Gotama? The Buddha replies, na gho aham vachcha evang dithi. No, accha, I am not of this view. Then vachcha puts the
opposite standpoint, which too, the Buddha answers in the negative. To all the ten questions, the Buddha
answers no, thereby rejecting the questioner in total. Then vachcha asks why, on seeing what danger, the Buddha
refuses to hold any of those leaves. The Buddha gives the following explanation.
Satsato loko ti kho vachcha dithi ghatamita, dithi ghana, dithi kantara, dithi visokam, dithi viphandita, dithi sanyojanam,
sadukha, savighatam, saupayasam, sa parilaha, na nibbidhaye, na viragaye, na nirodhaye, na upasamaye, na abhinyaye, na sambodhaye, na nibbhanaye, samadha.
Vachcha, this speculative vip, that the world is eternal, is a jungle of vips, a desert of vips, a distortion of vips, an aberration of vips, a fetter of vips.

It is fraught with suffering, with vexation, with despair, with delirium. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to tranquillity, to higher knowledge, to enlightenment, to nibbhan.
So with regard to the other nine vips. Now here we find both the above mentioned reasons. Not only the fact that these questions are not relevant to the attainment of nibbana,
but also the fact that there is something wrong in the very statement of the problems. What are the dangers that he sees in holding any of these vips?

Every one of them is just a speculative vips, the thigatam, a jungle of vips, the thiganam, an arid desert of vips, the thikantaram, a mimicry or distortion of vips, the thivisukam, an aberration of vips, the thiviphanditam, a fetter of vips, the thisanyojanam.

They bring about suffering, sadukham, vexation, savighatam, despair, saupayasam, delirium, sa parilaham. They do not conduce to disenchantment, na nibbhadaya, dispassion, na viragaya, cessation, na nirodhaya, to tranquillity, na upasamaya, to higher knowledge, na abhinyaya, to enlightenment, na sambodhaya, to extinguishment, na nibbhanaya.
From this declaration, it is obvious that these vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips, vips.
These questions are ill-founded and misconceived.
They are a welter of false tips, so much so that the Buddha even declares
that these questions simply do not exist for the noble disciple, who has hurt the dhamma.
They occur as grave problems only to the untaught worldly.
Why is that?
Whoever has a deep understanding of the four noble truths would not even raise these questions.
This declaration should be enough for one to understand why the Buddha refused to answer them.
Explaining that it is because of these dangers that he rejects them in total,
the Buddha now makes clear what his own stance is.
Instead of holding any of those speculative waves,
he has seen for himself the rise, samudaya, and fall, abthagama,
of the five aggregates as a matter of direct experience,
thereby getting rid of all eyeing and mying and latencies to conceits and winning ultimate release.
Even after this explanation, Vacha resorts to the fourfold logic
to satisfy his curiosity about the after-death state of the monk thus released in mind.
When the monk is thus released in mind, Master Gautama, where is he reborn?
The Buddha replies,
To say that he is reborn, Vacha falls short of a reply.
If that is so, Master Gautama, is he both reborn and not reborn?
To say that he is both reborn and is not reborn falls short of a reply.
If that is so, Master Gautama, is he neither reborn, nor is not reborn?
To say that he is neither reborn nor is not reborn falls short of a reply.
The Buddha, at this unexpected response of the Buddha to his four questions, Vacha confuses that he is fully confused and builded.
The Buddha grants that his confusion and buildement are understandable since this Dhamma is so deep and subtle
that it cannot be found that it cannot be found by logic.
However, in order to give him a clue to understand the Dhamma point of view, he gives an illustration in the form of a Ketachisara.
What do you think, Vacha, suppose a fire was burning before you, would you know this fire is burning before me?
If Master Gautama, if Master Gautama, a fire was burning before me, I would know this fire is burning before me.
If Master Gautama is burning before me, if Master Gautama is burning before me,
What does this fire that is burning before you, burn independence on?
Being asked thus, Vacha, what would you answer?
Evang puttho ahang bho Gautama evang pya kare iyaan.
Yomi ayang purato aggi jalati, ayang aggi tina katthu badanam paticca jalati iti.
Being asked thus, Master Gautama, I would answer this fire burning before me burns independence on grass and sticks.
Sache te vacche purato so aggi ni bha ye ye, yane yasithvang ayang me purato aggi ni bhutoti.
If that fire before you were to be extinguished, would you know this fire before me has been extinguished?
Sache me bho Gautama purato so aggi ni bha ye ye, yane yahan ayang me purato aggi ni bhutoti.
If that fire before me were extinguished, Master Gautama, I would know this fire before me has been extinguished.
Sache panatang vacha evang puchche ye, yote ayang purato aggi ni bhutoti so aggi ito kattamang disangato purathimangwa, pachimangwa, uttarangwa, dakhinangwa ati.
Evang puttho ko vacha kinti bhyakari yasi.
If someone were to ask you whatcha when that fire before you were extinguished, to which direction did it go to the east, the west, the north or the south?
Being asked thus, what would you answer?
Na upeti bho Gautama, yanghi so bho Gautama aggi tinaka dhupadanam pati cya jali, tasa cha pariyadana, anya sa cha anupahara, anaharo, nibbuto teo saṅkhanga chthiti.

That wouldn't do, as a reply master Gautama, for that fire burned independence on its fuel of grass and sticks that being used up and not getting any more fuel, being without fuel, it is reckoned as extinguished.
At this point a very important expression comes up, which we happened to discuss earlier too, namely saṅkhanga chthiti.
It means to be reckoned or to be known as, to be designated.
So the correct mode of designation in this case is to say that the fire is reckoned as extinguished and not to say that it has gone somewhere.
If one takes mean advantage of the expression, fire has gone out, and insists on locating it, it will only be a misuse or an abuse of linguistic usage.
It reveals a pervert tendency to misunderstand and misinterpret.
Therefore, all that can be said by way of predicating such a situation is nibbuto teo saṅkhanga chthiti.
It is reckoned as extinguished.
Now comes a well-timed declaration in which the Buddha, starting right from where Vachagata leaves off, brings the whole discussion to a climactic end.
Now comes a well-timed declaration in which the Buddha is the result of the Buddha.
Even so, watch that form by which
one designating the Sathagata might designate him,
yet has been abandoned by him,
auto-fed the root,
made like an uprooted palm tree,
made non-existent and incapable of arising again.
The Sathagata is free from reckoning in terms of fur, watcher.
He is deep, immeasurable and hard to fathom like the great ocean.
To say that he is reborn falls short of a reply.
To say that he is not reborn falls short of a reply.
To say that he is both reborn and is not reborn falls short of a reply.
To say that he is neither reborn nor is not reborn falls short of a reply.
This declaration, which a fully convinced Vachagata,
now wholeheartedly hailed and compared to the very hearthood of a solitary,
enshrines an extremely profound norm of Dhamma.
It was when Vachagata had granted the fact that it is improper to ask
in which direction an extinguished fire has gone
and that the only proper linguistic usage is simply to say that it is extinguished,
that the Buddha came out with this profound pronouncement concerning the five aggregates.
In the case of the Sathagata, the aggregate of form, for instance, is abandoned,
Pahinam, cut off at the root, Ucchinnamulam, made like an uprooted palm tree,
divested from its site, Talavathukatan, made non-existent, Anabhavakatan,
and incapable of arising again, Ayatim Anupadha Dhamma.
Thereby, the Tathagata becomes free from reckoning in terms of form,
Hupasamkha-vimutto-kho Tathagato.
Due to this very freedom, he becomes deep, immeasurable and unfathomable like the great ocean.
Therefore, he cannot be said to be reborn or not to be reborn or both or neither.
The abandonment of form, referred to above, comes about not by death or destruction,
but by the abandonment of craving.
The fact that by the abandonment of craving itself, form is abandoned or eradicated,
comes to light from the following quotation from the Radha Sanyukta of Sanyukta Nikkara.
Rūpe-kho-radha, yo-chandu, yo-raago, ya-nandi, ya-tanha,
ta'ng pajahat, evaṁ ta'ng rūpang pahīnaṁ bhavisati,
ucchinnamulam, talavathukatang, anabhavakatang,
ayatim Anupadha Dhamma.
Rather, you give up that desire, that lust, that delight, that craving for form.
It is thus that form comes to be abandoned, cut off at the root,
made like an uprooted palm tree, made non-existent and incapable of arising again.
Worldlings are under the impression that Anarang's five aggregates of grasping get destroyed at death.
But according to this declaration, Anarang is like an uprooted palm tree.
A palm tree, uprooted but left standing, divested of its sight,
might appear as a real palm tree to one who sees it from a distance.
Similarly, an untoward worldling thinks that there is a being or a person in truth and fact
when he hears the term Tathagata, even in this context too.
This is the insinuation underlying the above-quoted pronouncement.
It has some profound implications, but time does not permit us to go into them today.
